May I just ask you what your position is because the Chamber has great difficulties, I checked with the other Judges, to understand that if persons are a bit lower, they are not any higher anymore so if you take into consideration the -- that some extra fragments could hit people at a lower level, there are more fragments then at the same time these people are missing at a higher level to receive the fragments that are flying there. You understand what I mean? And therefore we have great difficulties in understanding your line of questioning and we noticed that the witness also has.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The position is that the -- perhaps the witness should be sent out, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we can ask the witness just to leave for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- before you explain, what my understanding, and I take it also the understanding of the other Judges is that of course if a person is at a lower level as the point of impact, the down-going fragments could hit that persons and on the horizontal level they would not be calculated. At the same time, all the fragments that are flying horizontally and that would hit that person if it was not at a lower level is not there anymore to be hit. So I don't know whether you calculated this all in because it -- but this is, I'm not an expert, but on the basis of, I would say, of normal reasoning it would see what you gain as possible area below the level you will miss it at a higher level.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, if I may, Mr. President, briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The purpose of the cross-examination is to indicate that the theoretical model the witness is using does not apply. One has to relate the evidence of this witness that persons, that two metres up, above two metre doesn't apply -- may I withdraw that and rephrase. His formulas would not apply to structures or persons higher than two metres. The explosion occurred one metre up. According to the witness it is about 70 centimetres down, centimetres or -- 17? He did give a figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which is less than two metres so horizontal particles would be hitting persons standing in the garden and the particles which his formula discounted that go downward would also be hitting persons sitting in the garden as is the evidence of Rasim Mehonjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes but at the same time the particles that would fly I would say up 50 centimetres that would normally hit a person if he was at the same level finds no person there anymore to be hit so therefore -- the witness was talking about the density of fragments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think that's the whole issue. He says we find a density of fragments at a certain distance which is there or there. Then of course you need objects to be hit by those fragments, whether they are low, so that the fragments did not end into the earth but could continue to fly or whether these person are a bit higher, perhaps you asked the witness whether it would influence the density of fragments because that's the whole issue and we really have great difficulties in following you -- apart from what the mathematical consequences of that would exactly be that if I have an explosion here and the people all a bit lower, then of course there might be a slight difference but they will be hit by the particles flying down but they will not be hit anymore by the particles flying horizontally so therefore the -- it's a -- you are entering into a very, very detailed discussion on which the witness seems to have no clue how to handle it and therefore I thought it wise to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well I'll move on but as I -- I'll move on. As I indicated though we still maintain that even on his evidence, those flying horizontally would be effective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but only for -- let's say 20 or 30 centimetres perhaps that part of the body that would be high enough to catch the horizontal flying fragments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, for example -- yes. I can imagine that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We see that the witness cannot cope with this and I understand why.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I will try to proceed as it pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, to avoid any problems with regard to this issue, I heard the Professor's testimony, he spoke about 70 centimetres and then two steps. We know that two steps, that's about 36 centimetres, that's twice 18, according to the norms so I would like to see the photographs now, perhaps to see whether this concerns two steps or not and to ask him this question because there is a significant difference here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that you will be able to find them during the next break and then you of course can put them to the witness. Please, madam usher, could you escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, going back to my last question, are you aware of the amount and density of people who were at the gate and in the vicinity of the pump in the yard?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're aware of the total number from these testimonies, on the basis of these testimonies, it's between 100 and 150. That was the figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were these 100 to 150 people?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were said to be in the water queue and then in the calculation you can see that we used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, I was asking about the gate and the area of the pump but I will move on. I'd like to ask a few questions about what you said in respect to the Markale incident. You said it was clearly an impact detonation, that's what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the explosion is concerned, yes, yes. Yes, I said it was an explosion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Occurred on the surface of the ground?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Which is what all the other witnesses stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Can you have a look at your figure 2.1 in your report -- 2.21 at page 20.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, it was not an explosion like that, it was not an on-the-ground explosion?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The figure 2.21 is a graphic depiction of the values used in calculating the depth of penetration of a projectile. It has nothing to do with -- it has no direct connection with Markale. It has to do with the calculation of the penetration depth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. When the mortar shell explodes, according to the page 12 of your report there is a frontal swathe which comprises two part, the first part being particles of the fuse and of the shell case, front ogival part near the mouth and the second part being fragments from the remaining portion of the case ogival and you show that in figure 2.13 that there is a frontal swathe of fragments.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it looks like. That's for under 120 millimetres, it's figure 2.13. It's for 120 millimetre shell, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the zone of lethal fragments for various drop velocities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to show you a photograph with the assistance of the usher. This is a high-speed x-ray photograph of the burst and fragmentation of a high-impact projectile. Is that a high-speed photograph -- x-ray photograph of the burst of a high-speed projectile?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a mortar shell, this is an artillery shell and it disintegrates, disperses in a way that is totally different in which a mortar shell disintegrates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I am asking basically -- very well, it is an artillery shell?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a photograph of an artillery projectile, a shell, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now what I wish to ask you is whether or not in the process of the shell bursting in what you describe here to be an artillery projectile you see in the photograph to the right the body of the projectile swells before it bursts?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the left, this is the projectile before it bursts, before it explodes and here, we have the stages when the process of explosion has commenced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I agree with you that an artillery shell disperses in a different way to the mortar shell, but wouldn't you agree with me that the mortar shell also expands, the jacket swells and expands before it bursts?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's such a rapid process, a few thousandths of a second but the basic thing you must know is that the photograph of a shell which is in the process of exploding isn't the same because an artillery projectile because of high acceleration, it's -- the thickness of the case increases at the bottom and in the case of the mortar shell, the dimensions of the body are smaller and in the photograph that I provided you with, you have the exact dimensions, they decrease.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the area of the fuse in the right photograph of the shell just before it explodes, you see the fuse also swells slightly. Would that also apply in respect to the burst of a mortar projectile?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fuse? No, that's impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In respect to the artillery shell here, you can see the fuse has expanded slightly.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of some artillery fuses that have a larger diameter, there can be deformations because of the shock wave, it can expand but in the case of mortar fuses, especially the M-62 which is used a lot in the former Yugoslavia, this can't happen. It can be ejected. The shock wave can eject it frontally, this happens very often. That's why we have such a clear impression of the fuse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I suggest to you that on explosion, in respect to the mortar shell, the fuse swells -- the fuse expands as well and is distorted by the blast of the explosion in a mortar shell; do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I just want to check the translation because -- it's as I said: If the diameter of the fuse is slightly greater, if it has the central part to penetrate but it will be affected by the shock wave because it's an aluminum construction so it would not really swell, it would not really expand. This is made of aluminum, the fuse is made of aluminum, the body of the fuse which is wound on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The photograph can be removed. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the shell at Markale exploded on the surface. Can you tell us what caused the crater?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every explosion results in the creation of a crater. If you put a shell on the -- an anti-tank shell on a concrete surface it will also cause a crater to be produced. If you're asking me about Markale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, I'm talking about -- I'm referring to your --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When a shell explodes on impact on the surface, what causes the crater? And maybe you could assist us in explaining that by looking at your figure 2.13.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crater is caused by a explosion of a mortar shell, if we're talking about a mortar shell. When the projectile impacts on the ground, on the surface, a crater is created primarily because of the effect of the front part of the fragments around the fuse and the fuse. That is the first impact which leaves the trace. And the second part is the part of the body, the fragments of a fragmented body of the shell will disperse and they will leave traces on the surface, that will depend, of course, on the type of the surface so there will be either more pronounced or less pronounced traces. So that will depend on the effect of the fuse. The crater could be of greater or lesser depth. That will depend on the fuse. If it is an instant fuse it will make a very, very small crater, very small crater. That will depend on the speed of the fuse and also how hard the surface is. If it is a very hard surface, the crater will be shallow. If it is softer than the crater will be deeper as I explained it yesterday, you can also see it on that photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have explained very well, thank you. So you know of Professor Vukasinovic's research into the explosion of mortar projectiles, you would be aware of it? You would be, yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not only do I know that, but I was professor of Vukasinovic and I spent my entire working life with him, I mean, we worked together and also while he was doing his doctoral thesis, I helped him with some consultations, Professor Stamatovic was his mentor and we jointly conferred in some things and he did his Ph.D thesis extremely well and he's known to be as one of our best experts in this area and I believe also in the world because his works are also accepted in America.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We'll get to his published work later. Would you agree with me that the crater of an impact or a contact detonation on the surface is caused by the frontal swathe of the products of a detonation as referred to at page 12 of your report, which is taken almost verbatim from some of his work?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So with an instant fuse as in the Markale incident, would you agree with me that the stabiliser does not penetrate the area where the crater -- or may I rephrase. In an explosion of a mortar shell with an instant fuse, if the stabiliser should lodge, it does not penetrate the top surface which is blasted away by the products of the detonation?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Coming back to the question what was the velocity of the projectile if the velocity of the -- the impact velocity of the projectile was higher than the velocity of the ejection of the stabiliser, then the stabiliser will continue to go in that direction; however, if the impact velocity was lesser, then the stabiliser would be ejected backwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Dr. Vilicic, that you did not understand the question. The question is that if a tail fin finally ends because it continues its trajectory, ends in the ground, that it will not be confronted by the resistance of the soil or whatever surface it is that has already been removed by the forces produced by the detonation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you understand that the first part of the path has already been paved by the explosion and will not create any resistance to the tail fin anymore. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, the interpretation was inadequate. I read the English transcript and your explanation now. So in the first part of the penetration, up to the instant fuse effect, the stabiliser is not involved in that stage. Later on, the stabiliser continues to move in that direction and hits that surface, the depth of the crater because of the fact that of the shell is not part of the stabiliser penetration. These are two separate functions. However, the crater, so that the stabiliser can go more deeply then the crater has to be deeper, if we measure the depth of penetration of the stabiliser depending on the surface, then the stabiliser, in order to penetrate deeply has to have higher velocity and has to have this depth of penetration will depend on the quality of the surface, of the resistance of the surface. Your question wasn't very clear. What did you want to know so that -- to clarify it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Vilicic, I think that you did not fully understand actually what Mr. Stamp wanted to know. Mr. Stamp wants to know whether the top layer of the surface on which a projectile lands has been blasted away already by the explosion itself so that it will not create any resistance once the tail fin, if it arrives with high enough speed, comes to the ground level.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As I said, the stabiliser and the projectile, these are two different stages. The crater caused by the projectile and the crater, the penetration of the stabiliser through the crater, these are two different -- two separate functions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to make it absolutely clear, witness, I'm using your report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has no unclarities in respect to the answer of the question just put first by you and -- if you get my meaning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For clarification, you gave us in table 4 of your report the muzzle velocity of fragments. While I suggest to you, and -- I suggest to you that the muzzle velocities that you have here are much lower than the muzzle velocities?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the velocity of the dispersion of the fragments, the average velocity of the fragment dispersion, table 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I do not understand your last question, but "while I suggest to you and I suggest to you that the muzzle velocities that you have here are much lower than the muzzle velocities."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Than the real time muzzle velocities for the 82 millimetre mortar -- I'm sorry the witness is not hearing. You just indicated that you didn't hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me suggest to you that the actual muzzle velocities for the 82 millimetre high explosive shell and the 120 millimetre high explosive shell are about two to three times higher than what you have here. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- to -- in order to avoid whatever confusion, table 4 gives mean values of muzzle velocities, I don't know whether you are referring to mean values or to maximum or minimum or...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mean values.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mean values, yes. So Mr. Stamp puts to you that the mean values indicated on page 9, table 4, are two to three times lower than they actually are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Higher, not smaller.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He's quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so therefore that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, I see, the question was quite properly put, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well there's -- in reality, there are two or three times higher and therefore represented the two to three times lower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the detonation explosion measured in our laboratory for TNT is 6.000 metres per second. That is the velocity of the shock wave. Now, the mean velocity of the fragments is calculated on the basis, on the basis of classification and the representatives of the group of fragments. When we have a projectile fragmenting, dispersing, the fragments are taken for calculation are taken for fragments that are of mass 1 gram to 50 grams, that's the group of the fragments depending on the calibre. What's calculated is value for the mean fragment and it is the value of that mean fragment is this mean velocity. Fragments move in different -- at different velocity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us assume that you are right and I am wrong. Would you agree with me though that at velocities that you have given here, the products of detonation would have created the crater before the stabiliser arrives?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, stabiliser is together with the projectile. The blast of the projectile, if the velocity, drop velocity is higher than the ejection of the stabiliser velocity, the stabiliser will continue its direction of movement or it will go back if the velocity is lower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Try to -- I'm -- I think what Mr. Stamp asks you is whether the fragments that result from the explosion of the shell, that the fragments have such a speed that they will create the crater, that is, that they will damage the soil on which the projectile lands prior to the arrival of the tail fin at that same surface. So that they are there first do the damage cause a crater and only afterwards the tail fin would arrive at that spot. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I agree with that. First the fuse hits and then there will be the frontal swathe of the fragments would hit because of the blast, they will create the crater. After that the stabiliser would arrive if it's velocity is higher as I've already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not blown back. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So a lot of the analysis has to do with the fuse setting. Now, at page 3 and at page 5 of your analysis, you indicate the fuse settings for the 82 millimetre mortar, there is impact and superquick and at page 5, for the 120 millimetre mortar, impact, superquick and delayed.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at page 18 of your report, you give us the specifications according to Yugoslav or JNA tests for a superquick fuse: "In modern" -- and I'm reading from the English version of your report, "In modern impact percussion fuses of superquick action, sensitivity is defined as target resistance that will surely activate the fuse"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are reading Mr. Stamp. That means you are quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I will start again. "In modern impact percussion fuses of superquick action, sensitivity is defined as target resistance that will surely activate the fuse. Usually it is a fir board about 25 millimetres thick and fuse reaction time is most frequently about one millisecond."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a correct rendition of what you have written?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's stated in the footnote, you have the literature is given that it's been quoted from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me that Krsic, Nikola Krsic was the only Yugoslav who has done research into fuse speeds or has written a book about it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Your figure of one millisecond comes from his 1967 work?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you used his estimation of time of one millisecond to apply to a modern impact percussion fuse of superquick action. That's what you did; is that so?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, on page 19 in the formula of the real penetration, if you take less time than one millisecond, you would get lower values for the depth of penetration. In other words, if we had taken the values that you're suggesting, we would have achieved even smaller craters, lower values in respect of the fuse effect. Say it's half a millisecond, then you will see how much the depth of penetration is lessened by that. That would be 0.5 thousandths of a second you will get much lower depth of penetration a much shallower crater when a shell explodes. In other words, we used less favorable values.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm simply asking you that your fuse activation time is a millisecond and that is based on Krsic's research.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not just that. We carried out a large number of experiments. We examined, analysed fuses, we have x-ray, we have a lab for ballistic examinations and analysis. If you -- if I had known that you needed such photographs, I would have brought photographs and x-rays of shells that we had done as well as of fuses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm speaking of fuse speeds, fuse speeds. Listen to me carefully it's very important. Listen to me. Listen to me, Professor, please.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by fuse speed? [In English] Reaction time of -- yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The speed of one millisecond you use in your calculations to formulate tables 7 and 8 at page 21 of your report?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one millisecond.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you use one millisecond, your results are that a 120 millimetre mortar at a relatively low-impact velocity of 121 metres per second would penetrate the ground to the extent of .63 metres before it explodes. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 7 centimetres, 7 centimetres it would penetrate 7 centimetres. The depth of penetration would be 7 centimetres. Under the angle of 47.3 degrees, it would be the impact velocity 121 metres per second, the depth of penetration without the fuse being activated, without an explosion, it would go 15, with the explosion it would go 10 deep and under the angle, the depth of penetration would be 7 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go through it a little bit more slowly. Look at table 7.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The third column from the left, what does that column signify?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are impact velocities, drop velocity of the projectile, that is, VC metres a second, these are drop velocities for 82 to 120, 122, impact velocity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the column to the right of that, with TR, that is a fuse speed?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the time of one millisecond.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fuse activation speed?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Time activation speed, reaction time of fuse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The column to the right of that LP, what is that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the depth, LP, the depth of penetration [In English] Penetration without function of fuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just one intervention, the transcript of the interpretation, the witness made it very clear, he made his position very clear by distinguishing the reaction and the activation and what's missing, there are two negative reactions in the transcript. We shouldn't confusion the notions. I think it's very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it then that we have paid proper attention to that and even someone who reads the French transcript will now read this observation. Please proceed then, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were telling us what the column with IP at the head means?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the depth of the penetration of the projectile without the functioning of the fuse. If the fuse malfunctions, that would be the depth of the penetration in the surface, in the soil. However, because it encountered resistance, the reaction happened after one millisecond, the realistic trajectory wouldn't be 18 it would be 6 centimetres because the fuse reacted and the projectile penetration then stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to create no confusion, Mr. Stamp, where you said IP, I particular it that you are referring to LP, I think it's LP if you would look at figure 2.21, you see it's written there with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's LP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at what point does a fuse activate and the explosion occurs in this table?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fuse is activated at the moment -- let's take your example, 120 millimetre mortar. 47.3 drop angle, 121 metre per second velocity, it would go without the fuse to the depth of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- But the complete projectile would go 12 centimetres into the soil so that the depth of the penetration is 9 centimetres, the depth of the crater would be 9 centimetres in that case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, the projectile would penetrate the soil to the degree of 9 centimetres and then explode?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It would create that crater, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is a different type of crater to the one where it explodes on impact on the surface.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand, what do you mean that that will be different?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A crater --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in order to avoid confusion, I don't think that certain things were heard well and are not in the transcript because of interpreters and I'm referring to page 62, line 23, what I said was that in the English transcript, there are two negative answers of the witness. It's exactly the opposite negative answers missing [In English] Missing thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's 12:30, we'll have a break for 20 minutes. Mr. Stamp, I got the feeling that on your last few questions, there was great misunderstanding between you and the witness. Perhaps you could -- either he didn't understand you well or you didn't understand his answers well, but I got the feeling that there was great misunderstanding. Perhaps you could formulate your questions in such a way that we avoid -- I know that it's witness and those who examine the witness together but let's try to avoid confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I would endeavour to articulate my questions with clarity. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until ten minutes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just say something? Yesterday, you gave me a homework to -- if that's possible, to make a drawing of the change of velocity with the height and I did that with a lot of pleasure but with the limitation because I didn't have all the calculations and the right table. What I did is that I made an approximate drawing but if you need it in ten days or so I can send it, a computerised calculation but if you want I -- this can be copied for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would certainly have come back to that because I asked you so I -- if you would please give it to madam usher so that it can be copied and I already thank you very much for assisting us also in this respect. We'll adjourn until ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Vilicic, these are long days but we have to continue. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness -- I'm sorry, Professor?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the resistance to penetration of a fir board is lower than the resistance to penetration of concrete?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Can I explain? A board, a fir board is used when developing a fuse. It's the minimum resistance provided that a fuse should react if the projectile goes through the board and the fuse isn't activated then that means that the fuse isn't functioning properly and those sort of fuses are rejected but this is something that we use in the course of developing new fuses. This has nothing to do with -- it hasn't direct [Realtime transcript read in error "has indirect"] relation with subsequent events. It's a matter of changing the time of reaction, the fuse reaction time. It's a one-inch fir board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 24.5 millimetres fir board?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one saw, one inch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me see if I understand what you just explained. In the tests for the fuse sensitivity, it would have to explode, detonate the mortar before it passes through the fir board, that's how it is tested.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sorry. That's the minimum pre-condition for fuse to be sure. When it hits such a board it mustn't react at the time and this is only checked when you are deciding whether to adopt a certain fuse to use -- accept certain fuses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Professor, Professor, please. Have a look on page 65, line 9, it says, "This has nothing to do with -- it has indirect relation." I think the translation was: "It hasn't direct relation".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it doesn't have a relation. The characteristic of the security of the fuse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The purpose of the test is to ensure that the fuse is surely activated before it passes through that fir board, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the purpose of this test is that at a certain distance from the barrel muzzle, the projectile mustn't react when hitting the board. This confirms that it is functioning properly so that it should not explode, the shell should not explode in the barrel, et cetera. You asked me whether the resistance of the board was greater or equal to that of concrete and that's why I said that the two things had nothing to do with each other. A fir board is its resistance to the action of fragments, a one-inch fir board is used to test how many fragments can penetrate it and if a one-inch fir board is penetrated by these fragments then one concludes that the resistance is of a certain kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll read part of your report and ask you to explain what it means. "In modern impact percussion fuses of a superquick action, sensitivity is defined as target resistance that will surely activate the fuse,"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Stamp please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are reading, Mr. Stamp and I think we'd like to have the page reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Page 18, I beg your pardon. Page 18, line 7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "In modern impact percussion fuses of superquick action, sensitivity is defined as target resistance that will surely activate the fuse. Usually it is a fir board 25 millimetres thick." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a manner of testing how sensitive the fuse is. The board corresponds to the energy that is needed to activate the fuse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, the fuse, if I may put it that way, successfully passes the test of being a superquick or a fuse of superquick action if it surely activates before passing through that fir board?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If it is activated when coming into contact with the board, yes, but there are two concepts that we must distinguish. One is testing the safety of the fuse to ensure that it is safe when in the barrel and the second function is on a board in front of the muzzle six, seven, eight metres, it mustn't be activated and afterwards, after that it has to react when it comes into contact with the one-inch board so that from moment in time it means that the mechanisms are functioning, they were active so that the next time a superquick fuse hits a board it has to react. At a distance of 8 metres it has to pass through such a board and at a distance of 15 metres, it has to be activated, the fuse has to explode.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before it passes through the board?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. When it comes into contact with the board, it penetrates the screen in any event but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Back to your tables at page 21 and that is table 8. You will see in the rows for the mortar shell of 120 millimetre that your calculation of depth or depth up to the point of explosion which is in the right column, the furthest right column indicate penetration depths all of which are greater than the 2.45 millimetres for the fir board test.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, table 8 has nothing to do with fir boards, this has to do with concrete. It's the depth of craters when the surface is a concrete one. You have to make a distinction between the sensitivity, that is the time at which something is activated and the time when this happens. When hitting this board, one hasn't defined where the projectile was when the explosion occurred. All that was requested, all that was requested was that it should be activated. These two things cannot be related to each other, cannot be linked up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does column -- the right-hand column in table 8, the furthest right column in table 8 speak to?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It indicates the -- let's say the altitude of the depth of penetration, the distance from the lowest point, the distance of the lowest point from the surface since the projectile entered at a given angle and this first example, it's 46.5 degrees, that's the drop angle so for a trajectory of 10 centimetres, when you divide the altitude with the drop angle with the sinus, you get the altitude, go back to the image you asked me about, figure 2.21.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this column to the right, furthest right of table 8 indicating the penetration depth in concrete before the fuse activates and the projectile explodes?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's the total penetration depth, the elevation H. H is the total number of -- in metres of the depth of penetration when the fuse was activated because H is calculated LPR through sine, LPR and the sine of this factor you can see that H through LP, LPR is the sine of the drop angle that is this Delta C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I think that the attitude of the Prosecution which seeks to affirm something different from what we can see quite clearly in the expert report, I don't think this attitude is acceptable. One can cross-examine is fine but to simply claim the opposite in our opinion this is not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have the feeling that there's some misunderstanding as to the table, the understanding of the table, Mr. Stamp. May I try. Do I understand you well that that the last column on page 21, table 7 indicates the depth of the hole that is caused by a mortar shell landing and exploding and has got nothing to do which whatever is left in the soil but just the depth of the hole created by the explosion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what we see on several pictures we see apart from markings of several fragments we see in the centre just a small hole and this is the depth of the hole once the projectile has landed and has exploded irrespective of whatever could be still found, has got nothing to do with that, whether later a tail fin or the fuse would, I take it that the fuse would be destroyed also but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that clear -- is that clarifying anything, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, to some degree, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I hope it did. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do your tables here in respect to the 120 millimetre mortar shell here in this column indicate the depth of penetration before the fuse is activated?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they don't. LP, the LP column corresponds to the depth of penetration of the projectile if the fuse fails to activate, if the fuse doesn't function properly. [In English] Longer of penetration, not depth, longer of penetration, LP, highest depth of penetration, longer of penetration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And LPR, that column, what is that column showing?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the time reaction of the fuse, it indicates that if the fuse is functioning, the projectile will, for example in the column instead of penetrating on the ground 15 centimetres it will penetrate to a depth of 10 centimetres because it will explode at -- after having covered 10 centimetres and that will be the depth so that is the trajectory of the projectile up until the time in which it explodes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So if the depth of penetration is smaller when the fuse is activated than when the projectile penetrates the ground without the fuse being activated so the depth of penetration is not as great as when the fuse is activated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction, when the fuse fails to function properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So LPR tells you the depth that the projectile will travel until the fuse is activated?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] It's not depth, it's --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or the measurement of penetration then that the projectile will travel before?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's longer of penetration, longer of penetration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Length?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Longer of penetration. Depth of penetration is H.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you, Dr. Vilicic, I have to correct myself first because everyone correctly says Professor Vilicic. I should have done that during the last two days as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's because of the name. Professor Vilicic, could you please, on a piece of paper, just draw what LPR is because I have no difficulty understanding H, no difficulty in understanding LP, but LPR is still ... If you could do it on the ELMO, we could follow you, so if it's not too inconvenient.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the surface, ground surface. The projectile falls at an angle theta C, from this point in time it starts penetrating the ground. If the fuse is not activated, let's assume that the projectile reaches this point and this is the length, the LP length. It depends on the resistance and characteristics of the ground. If, as is usual, the fuse is activated, the fuse will be activated after one millisecond. If it is activated after an even shorter period of time then the depth will be even smaller. Let's say this is when the fuse exploded. This length represents the length of the penetration, LPR, this is where the explosion occurred, and this is the real depth of the crater so this is the point that the projectile reached if the fuse activated. If it failed to activate then it would have penetrated to this point. LPR, this value is given in the formula on page 19 and you can see it's -- the drop velocity, the time of reaction of the fuse, so it's VCTR through 4 LP, one minus VCTR to 4 LP if this is reduced then the LP, if the LP is reduced you can see what the calculation is, the impact velocity, this is VC. If in this equation you reduce TR, then the value for LPR is also reduced. In other words, if we had taken a long period of time, well, in fact we took a less favorable case when analysing the penetration than would have been the case with the superquick modern fuse which would have been activated after 5 milliseconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you tell us as a matter of fact --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After half a millisecond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Which each is I would say the projection, the length of the projection upwards to the surface of LPR.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vertical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The vertical distance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vertical distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the surface whereas LPR is the real distance as the fuse has travelled before exploding and what is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Projectile, projectile. I'm sorry. [In English] Before explosion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before explosion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what is confusing a little bit is that LP on your sketch is relatively short where it is approximately 6 to -- 6 times longer than LPR usually according to your -- according to your table or at least a couple of times it's only a little bit longer on your sketch. Mr. Stamp, is it clear to you now what LPR is?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, very clear. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. And may I ask you one additional question because I take it that it's all about that, the quicker the fuse activates upon reaching the soil, the smaller the value of LPR and therefore also of H will be; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have it that you said: "If in this occasion you reduce TR then the value for LPR is also reduced. In other words if we had taken a long period of time well in fact we took a less favorable case when analysing the penetration than would have been the case with superquick modern fuses which would have been activated after 5 milliseconds."

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, clear. The shorter the time, the less penetration there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there is a problem of interpretation or reading. It's 0.5 milliseconds not 5 milliseconds as the Prosecution states now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we are talking about one millisecond or half a millisecond which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is why I reread the transcript to him to correct it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Half a millisecond.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words the superquick fuses reaction time are faster than the times in these tables. The superquick fuses -- you nodded, could you answer verbally? The superquick fuses reaction times are faster than the ones used for these tables; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Superquick fuses, yes, but they have a completely different structure to these fuses. They are completely different fuses, not these fuses we are talking about here, these are mechanical fuses that are installed on the projectiles but the superquick fuses are used for projectiles and they are electrical fuses. On Yugoslav shells you don't have such fuses. On shells, mortar shells of such manufacture there is no such fuses there are other fuses that can be activated during the trajectory but this is -- there are not such fuses used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know. When you say superquick fuses being one of the things is that can be used for the 80 millimetre and 120 millimetre mortar round, are you referring to a fuse that impacts on contact, that is, on contact with a surface without penetration?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we explained it in our expert report, it depends on the surface resistance. For the fuse to become activated for normal fuses, you need the certain amount of energy to be created to have the fuse becoming activated. In superquick fuses, the thing is also there has to be a contact with the surface but on mortar shells there are no such fuses. These are mostly the fuses that are on anti-tank projectiles, anti-tank projectiles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest to you that the superquick fuses which you refer to at page 18 which will surely activate before they penetrate a 25 millimetre board are fuses that were used by the JNA in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our official name for our fuse is ultra instant fuse which is UTM62. It's a quick fuse but it's not the most modern fuse. You spoke of superquick fuses. You commented on Krsic's data but our fuses are the ones that are relevant for those norms and that was the criteria for us for a superquick fuse. That was our criteria.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest to you that the Yugoslav superquick fuse which must surely activate before it penetrates a 25 millimetre fir board activates at a much faster speed than one millisecond.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very good if that's so, then all our calculations will have lesser depth of penetration instead of these values, you have lower values. The H and the LPR will be lower. I said that we used one millisecond and we could have reduced that if we had wanted it. If we had said that we had the most modern fuses but we know that our series of manufacture of fuses particularly old ammunition, they worked for one millisecond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Vilicic, may I ask you one question just in between? You said, "That's very good if that's so," good for what, good for whom? Would you explain what you meant by saying, "That's very good," if that was so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gentleman said that the lower time for the -- the functioning time is less than one milliseconds, 0.5 milliseconds now if we take 0.5 milliseconds then there would be less depth of penetration so the results would be even more favorable from the aspect they would be more favorable for -- when I mean favorable, let me just explain. What I mean by favorable is that you will have lower values so there will be less depth of penetration, everything will be lower in that sense it will be more favorable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, why would that be good or bad? I mean why are lower values any better than higher values?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there would be less depth of penetration automatically. That would mean there would be just shallower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why -- let me just ask you what -- why is less penetration better than more penetration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the point of view of the effectiveness of a projectile, it is greater if the projectile, for troops, if it explodes on the surface so if it is instant explosion when it touches, impacts on the surface, that's better. The effectiveness of projectile is better when it penetrates you have less depth of penetration because the higher depth of penetration, the less is the projectile effective but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is that is good for the effectiveness of the shell landing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, Professor, your table 7 and table 8 --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- On page 21 do not apply, the fuses that detonate on impact?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean "do not apply"? Because they apply as soon as there is one millisecond, these are calculations for the assumption that the time functioning of the projectile is one millisecond and these values apply for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also, in order to avoid confusion, what you are telling us that if you change TR in your tables, that the other columns will give different values.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What will change will be the LPR and H, they will be smaller. They will be lower values if TR is lower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I further suggest to you that, as you have said, a mortar round is more effective for persons -- well, effective against persons in the open when it explodes on impact and that was the normal fuse setting in the JNA and in Yugoslavia in the early 1990s, impact.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand this question. I don't know what you meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. When a fuse -- when a mortar projectile detonates on impact, it is more effective against troops in the open and that is why you said it was good?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it penetrates to a lesser degree, yes, the depth of penetration, the length of penetration reduces the effectiveness of the projectile but, I'm sorry, but I have an impression that you are confusing something. The table 7 and 8 are to do with craters with the length of penetration. These lengths, these depths are not related with the effectiveness of the projectile. These are the values for the length of penetration. They would be lower --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting to you is that there were impact fuses in use by the JNA in the early 1990s and by impact fuses, I mean fuses that exploded on contact with the ground.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one's contesting that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And these are the superquick fuses that, in your report, at page 3 and 5 you say are applicable to mortars?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, there seems to be a great confusion and I'd like to interfere. If you are talking about detonating upon impact, you are putting this as being exactly the same as superquick detonation, et cetera, et cetera. We have heard a lot of evidence which means the distinction between detonation on impact and for example delayed detonation so therefore I would put the following question to you, Professor Vilicic, when we are talking about fuses with a TR time of half a millisecond or one millisecond or a little bit higher or a little bit lower, would you still call all these fuses fuses used for detonation upon impact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are fuses that are used, UTU-M62 or UTU-M78, these are impact instantaneous fuses, that's what we call them, they are superquick, that's how it was translated into English. Ultra instant fuses. They can be ultra quick and with a time delay so they have a double action, that's what we call them, that would be the ultra instantaneous or if the relevant tap is turned on the fuse then this is done for a purpose, for the shell to penetrate more deeply into the soil, and that function of the fuse is used on 120 mortar shell fuses when we want to have -- to destroy something, this is not used for troops, this is used when we want to dig in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you would still talk about detonation upon impact if you would use any of the fuses you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Both fuses have this instant, instantaneous function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] English transcript, previous page line 15 so that the methods are clear, the witness said in the first part of the answer the opposite of what appears in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What the witness said at line 15, as a matter of fact, I did not only listen to the translation but I also looked at the witness when he said that, it should be checked in the original tape before it could be accepted that he said something different and perhaps that should be done if you claim that it's wrongly translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm simply talking about the first word, the rest of the reply it can be deduced, the rest of the answer is correct that he said that no one contested or something like that but the first part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood: "No, no one's contesting that." That is that -- but if you say that the answer is that no one contests that then let's forget about the first no because that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It was "yes, no one contest".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's then clear. I think everyone understood it in that sense. No, Mr. Stamp, I am looking at the clock but if you --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My suggestion is that when using fuses that detonate the mortar projectile on impact without penetration, the fuse time is much faster than those that you have used in this table.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be a shorter time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object, Mr. President for the simple reason that the witness just gave us a technical information on the changeable character of such a fuse; therefore, we cannot ask a general question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you could ask a question because there's one value used in the table so therefore, if there is a variety of possible fuses and if you use one in a table you can ask a question about the table. Let me just ask you, Professor Vilicic, what Mr. Stamp wants to know from you is whether the 1.0, the one millisecond you used in table 7 and table 8, that that is not the time which would be valid for the quicker or the quickest fuses used in the former JNA and that was used in mortars used during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the time that we officially used. This value is our value. This is a time constant which was used for ultra-instantaneous fuse function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask you the following: Are there any quicker fuses -- were there any quicker fuses used during the conflict, the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, this fuse function, this time for functioning time is measured when the new fuse is adopted, when it is created, when it is established, and we had that at the institute and our mean value for that was one millisecond. I don't know that in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- the question is quite simple. Were there any fuses used in mortar projectiles that had a quicker TR than the one you used in this table?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For mortar shells, this is the functioning time of the fuse that were manufactured in the former Yugoslavia and with which the mortar projectiles manufactured in Yugoslavia were equipped with and I am surprising where this data comes from because this is what we did at the institute. Where does this data come from that Yugoslavia had some other quicker fuses than these ones?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, Professor Vilicic is no, there was no quicker fuses used than the one with TR of one millisecond.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I just say something, mechanical fuses, this has to be said, because there are also electrical fuses but not for mortar projectiles, the mechanical fuses for Yugoslav projectiles for mortar shells had this functioning time of one millisecond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there are no quicker ones as you told us used in mortar bombs. The original of your homework may be returned to you but I would have one additional question. Could this, and it's available for the parties as well, could this be put on the ELMO just for one second? Professor Vilicic, I tried to set out a bit clearer what I asked you to do. I might have been not very clear so therefore I thought it better to write it down. You understand what is on this drawing? Your answers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Yes as they appear in the homework product you gave to us uses an increase of Y, you have increased Y with 500 metres and then you have answered the question of the velocity. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a heightened velocity if the weapon is 500 metres higher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that there is a relation between the two but I would like to have the difference in velocity expressed as a function of X rather than a function of Y because you said with an extra 500 metres Y you get this velocity and what I would like to know is with a 100 metres or 200 metres or 300 metres higher point of -- I know that they are related, but we, as lawyers, are not smart enough to translate what you gave us into the values we need. So if you could do the homework again, but not by referring to an extra trajectory Y but by extra trajectory X. Would that be possible or minor ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would request, I said that before and I would like to say that the equipment that I have doesn't allow me to do this at the moment because I only have a calculator, I don't have a computer to calculate the trajectory. If you need precise values, this can be done and then it can be forwarded through the Defence to the Trial Chamber. Here, on the table that I gave you, it will be possible to provide for each charge that would be a function Y of the drop velocity and dependent on the curve change, I extrapolated the curve and you've asked me for 500 metres. I made it for 500 metres negatively so that the weapon is higher than the target but if the weapon is below the target then this curve will go instead of right it will go to the left 500 metres and this is how you will get that velocity value. I don't have the original here to show on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be -- I understood your homework to be that you added 500 metres to the longitudinal trajectory and what I would like to have and I know that the values are related, I would very much like to have the difference in velocity when the level of impact would be higher that of course also would shorten the Y.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we are misunderstanding each other. This is Y, meaning 500 metres of altitude, not longitudinal, not a trajectory, it's a vertically 500 metres vertical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you did exactly what I asked you and at least the confusion has now been stopped. Yes, Professor Vilicic, as you might have noticed we have not finished yet, we will try to finish your testimony tomorrow and we'll adjourn until then, until 9.00 in the morning, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 1.55 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday the 28th day of February, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
